  declared a C local of its own, though the local is one variable for the
  function. `if k > 0 { n = 1 } else { n = 2 }` then `rebind = || { n = 7 }`
  and `rebind()` left `n` at 1, and the same for strings and arrays. Such
  a closure now writes the variable (#2901).

- **An optional or sum local a `try` body writes keeps the value after the
  catch.** Every other variable a `try` body writes is declared `volatile`,
  so the panic's longjmp cannot leave it in a register; an `int?`,
  `long?`, struct or `fn?` optional local, and a sum local, were not, and
  at -O1 and -O2 the catch and the code after it read the value from
  before the `try` (an `int?` gave -1 for 50), on both C paths. Their
  declarations now take the qualifier (#2902).

- **A tuple destructure rebinds a closure local.** `f = || { return 1 }`,
  then `f, n = pair(5)` where `pair` returns a closure and an int, then
  `call(f)` ran the first literal again: the call was emitted as a direct
  call of that literal's function, as if `f` had never been rebound. A
  destructure slot now counts as a binding of the variable wherever the
  direct-call shortcut is decided, so the call goes through the closure
  the variable holds (#2903).

- **Closures into `ptr` locals and state, zeroed state, `ptr` fields from
  strings.** A closure stored into a `ptr` local (as a rebinding or as its
  initializer) or into a `ptr` state field did not compile; it is now
  boxed there, and a bare function stored as its code address, as in every
  other `ptr` slot. A `state fn kept` (or a struct, optional, tuple or sum
  state field) with no initializer was set with `= 0`, which C refuses for
  those; it is now zeroed whole. A struct literal whose `ptr` field took a
  `ptr` local holding a string named a `_heap_<field>` tracker the struct
  does not have; a `ptr` field takes the pointer, which its source keeps
  (#2904).

- **The plain C path has no GNU statement expression left in the sweep.**
  Four `string?` constructs (a `string?` parameter a closure writes, a
  destructure into a `string?` cell or module var, a `??` over a `string?`
  local returned) were still spelled as statement expressions whatever the
  C compiler, so cl.exe and a strict C11 compiler rejected the programs
  using them. A cell or global now binds the value and then takes its
  string as a statement, and the returned `??` is a sequence of
  temporaries declared ahead of the return, as the rest of that path is.
  CI's strict C11 step now checks the C of every program the sweep builds,
  reading the C the sweep kept (`AE_SWEEP_KEEP_C=1`, ae's `AE_KEEP_C`), so
  a later construct cannot bring one back unseen (#2885).

- **`os.run_full`, `os.run_capture` and `run_capture_status` are safe to call from several threads at once (#2917).** A child inherited every inheritable handle the process held when it started: on Windows `CreateProcessW` ran with `bInheritHandles` and no handle list, and on POSIX the pipes had no close-on-exec flag. A child another thread started while a capture's pipes were open kept their write ends, so that capture waited for EOF until the unrelated child exited, seconds or forever. Each child now inherits its own stdio ends and nothing else (`PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST`; `pipe2(O_CLOEXEC)`).

- **A function of one clause can take a string literal pattern.**
  `only_hi("hi") -> int { ... }` emitted the literal into the C as a bare
  identifier, so the program did not compile ("'hi' undeclared"). Its
  check compares by content now, NULL-safe, as a clause set's dispatcher
  does (#2467), so a counted string with the same characters matches
  (#2913).

- **A string reaches every C extern as its characters.** An argument in
  a C-variadic extern's `...` (`printf(fmt, s)`) was passed as it is held,
  so a string built at run time formatted its AetherString header (#2914).
  An extern bound to another symbol (`@extern("sym") name(...)`) had its
  parameters looked up by that symbol, which the extern table does not
  file entries under, so none of its `string` arguments were unwrapped;
  std.strbuilder's `append_format` formatted a counted format string's
  header (#2915). A call finds its extern by the Aether name now, and a
  string in a vararg position is unwrapped as a declared `string`
  parameter is.

- **A panic releases what each place holds, once.** The unwind journal now
  records places (a string local, a temporary, a struct local) by address
  where they are declared, and a panic releases what each holds at that
  moment. It used to record values: once two places could hold the same
  string, a release forgot the other place's entry, so a caught panic leaked
  a string or released one twice. The drain also no longer runs a release
  while it walks the journal (#2923).

- **Arguments and temporaries outlive what uses them.** A string read from
  a module `var` or a field and passed to a function is held by the caller
  for the call, so a store into that place inside the call no longer frees
  the argument. A fresh string passed to a call that returns a view of it
  (`string.bytes(make())`) lives to the end of its statement, as a
  temporary does in C++; it was freed as the call returned, and the view
  read freed memory (std.cryptography's argon2 hashed garbage). A field
  read ahead of a call holds a reference of its own (#2920).

- **Structs, tuples, optionals and fixed-size arrays own what they hold.**
  Each owning type has one generated retain and one drop, used by every
  place: a tuple, optional or array local, a struct or tuple field, a module
  `var`, an array or slice element, a message field, a discard (`_ = v`).
  A tuple local held its strings without releasing them, an alias of it
  shared them, a struct stored into a module `var` leaked the one it
  replaced, an array local rebound in a loop leaked its elements, and a
  store through a slice leaked the element it replaced. A struct parameter
  borrows its caller's value, and one the body writes into is copied on
  entry (#2921).
- **A call through a closure value calls the closure it holds.** A local
  bound to a function's result was taken to hold the closure that
  function's first `return` gave, and was called directly; a function that
  returned another closure on another path crashed (#2921).

- **A `defer` runs when a caught panic leaves its scope.** The language
  reference says a plain `defer` runs on every exit; a panic skipped it, so
  `defer list.free(l)` in a `try` body, or in a function a panic passed
  through, leaked the list. While its scope is live a plain `defer` is now
  in the unwind journal, and a panic runs it there, newest first, over the
  locals as they are at that moment (#2923).
- **A caught panic releases each owning array, cell and argument.** A
  `string[N]` or struct array local, a variable a closure writes (its
  shared cell), an argument a call holds for its duration, and an `x!`
  error string handed to the catcher were not released when a panic left
  them (#2923).

- **A fixed-size array goes wherever a value goes.** A message field holds
  one by value and owns its elements; an optional wraps one
  (`let o: string[2]? = [...]`); an array literal of owning elements passed
  to a function is a temporary of its statement; one thrown away
  (`_ = [...]`) is dropped. These did not compile (#2921).
- **An element store into an owning array local takes its value.**
  `xs[0] = f` on a `fn[N]` or tuple array local leaked what the element held
  (#2921).
- **A `string?`, tuple or struct message field takes its value.** A send
  shared the sender's string with the message, and the receiver's release
  freed it under the sender (#2922).

- **A string local always owns what it holds.** The per-variable ownership
  flag (`_heap_<name>`) and the escape walk that kept a value alive when it
  might be stored are gone: every take hands the local a reference, a store
  releases the old value, a scope exit releases what is left, and a string
  given to C's memory (a header struct's field, a C view, an `@retain`
  extern) is given a reference of its own. A parameter the body rebinds
  takes its own reference on entry (#2920).
- **Whether a call hands back a string is read from its signature.** An
  Aether function returning `string`, or an extern returning `-> string
  @heap` or `-> ptr @heap`, hands its caller one reference; the body-walking
  return classifiers and the producer name list are gone, and the std
  constructors returning a counted string as `ptr` (`string.from_int` and the
  like, `string_new_with_length` wherever it is declared) say `@heap` (#2920).
- **No ownership decision reads another function's body.** The closure
  environment scan, the hand-back walks, the parameter escape walk and the
  copy-on-keep query are deleted; a closure cell always owns its closure, so
  a cell passed to a call that hands it back no longer pins it (#2788).
- **A builder that never names its config releases it** at its exit (#2871).
  Through a binary import the program releases it instead: a library's
  catalog (schema 1.8) marks such builders, and the import's stub passes
  them no config, so a library linking its own runtime never frees memory
  the program's runtime made (#2860). `ae lib-info` shows the mark as
  `config: never used`.
- **A string sequence is owned by every place that holds it.** A sequence
  passed to a function other than a `string.seq_*` op, returned, built from
  a call argument or holding a freshly built literal element was never
  released; a function returning its parameter handed back a reference it
  did not take. Every place now takes and releases its own reference, the
  std producers say `-> *StringSeq @heap`, and freeing a borrowed sequence
  parameter is refused (E0901) (#2921).
- **`list.add`, `list.set` and `map.put` keep a string a `-> ptr @heap`
  constructor returns** (`string.from_int(i)`): the container held freed
  memory once those constructors said `@heap` (#2920).
- **A string argument read from a field or an element is evaluated once.**
  The call took its own reference to the value and then read the place
  again, so a place built by calls (`f(make_item(w)).name`) ran them twice
  and leaked the first results (#2920).
- **A closure literal passed to a function taking a builder's `_ctx`**
  (`spec.it(...) callback { }`) is released after the call; every
  capturing callback leaked its environment (#2921).
- **`sort.strings` and `sort.strings_by` permute without taking or
  releasing** (`mem.swap_ptrs`), so sorting a C-owned `strarr` no longer
  copies and leaks its elements (#2920).
- **A receive arm's string binding, or a list pattern's head, that the arm
  rebinds takes a reference of its own first**: the rebind released the
  message's string, which the message released again (#2920).
- **A string stored into C memory viewed as `string[]` takes no
  reference**: the program keeps it alive while C reads it, and storing a
  string built in the same statement is refused (E0902), since nothing
  would keep it (#2926).
- **`pqueue.push` takes its item `@keep`** (the queue keeps it past the
  call): a string goes in through `string.keep(s)` and comes back out
  through `string.release_kept`. A string literal may be given to any
  `@keep ptr` as it is, being pinned (#2926).
- **`free(s)` of a string releases it as `release(s)` does**, leaving the
  place empty: a string local freed with the builtin (`defer free(home)`
  after `io.getenv`) was released again at its scope exit (#2920).
- **`string.free` of a place frees the place's own reference.** An `@retain`
  parameter took a reference of its own for the call, so a free through
  `string_free` released only that one and the place kept the string; a
  slice element is emptied as it is freed, as a field is (#2920).
- **A parameter or pattern binding the body rebinds no longer releases its
  owner's value** for tuples, optionals, closures and sequences (#2921).
- **A chain of closures, each holding the one before, is released in
  constant stack.** 50,000 rebinds to a closure calling the closure it
  replaced overflowed the stack on Windows when the chain was released
  (#2921).
- **`catch _` releases a panic reason built at run time**, which it kept
  before (#2920).
- **`tests/leaks_known.txt` is deleted**: every regression program reports 0
  leaks under the macOS gate, the OpenSSL test included (the cryptography
  module keeps the providers it loads) (#2925).

## [0.817.0]

### Fixed

- **An untyped const array whose first element is not a bare literal is an
  array of its elements' type.** `const T[] = [-1, 2, 3]` (or `[0 - 1, ...]`,
  `[~1, ...]`, `[-1.5, 2.0]`) was taken for an array of `ptr`: its first
  element had no type yet when the parser guessed, so it was emitted as
  `static const void* T[] = {...}`, which clang refuses (gcc only warned)
  and which read back as pointers (`x = T[0]` was a `void*`). The parser now
  leaves the element type unknown and marks the declaration inferred, and
  the typechecker gives it the literal's type once the elements are typed.
  Found by ae3d's shader call table (`const CALL_ARGS[] = [-1, -1, -1, 2,
  ...]`), which built with gcc and not with Apple's clang.

## [0.816.0]

### Added

- **`@quotable` functions: helpers a quote can call (std.quote version 2).**
  A function marked `@quotable` is ordinary Aether whose body is also a tree.
  A quote's call of one is a `HELPER_CALL`, and the quote's tree carries every
  `@quotable` function its body reaches, callees first
  (`quote.helper_count`/`helper`/`helper_named`, each a `quote.Tree` with
  `function_name` and `return_type`), so a back end can write each out as a
  function of its own (ae3d's GLSL). The quote's hash covers each helper it
  reaches, so editing a helper invalidates a cache keyed on the hash. A
  helper's body is checked against the quote subset where it is defined; one
  that reaches itself through `@quotable` calls is E0804 (GLSL and MSL have
  no recursion), and one that reads a variable outside it is E0805.
  `quote.VERSION` is 2, and the format version is in the hash, so **every
  quote's hash changes once**: regenerate anything cached under it (ae3d:
  `build/generate_shaders`).

## [0.815.0]

### Fixed

- **Stopping the scheduler destroys each core's locks, so a scheduler run
  again leaks nothing on Windows.** `scheduler_init()` made each core's park
  and foreign-send locks again without the previous run's being destroyed.
  On Windows a critical section that has been contended holds a 48-byte heap
  block until it is deleted, so every run in which a wake met a core at its
  park, or two threads off the cores sent at once, lost one per lock. The
  scheduler teardown heap test failed the 0.813.0 Windows release build with
  it (240 then 480 bytes) and about one run in 40 locally. The locks are now
  destroyed with the core tables, and a new test contends a core's lock in
  every cycle, so the loss shows on each run instead of by chance.

## [0.814.0]

### Fixed

- **`sandbox.enforce` no longer leaves the sandbox on after its block.** It
  uninstalled the checker before popping its grant list, and uninstall clears
  the checker only when no list is left, so the checker stayed installed for
  the rest of the process. Its check then allowed everything (no list), but
  the path resolution in front of it still ran: after any `enforce`, a fs call
  on a path that cannot be resolved (a dangling symlink, say) was refused
  with "sandbox: cannot read path" outside every sandbox, and
  `fs.fs_is_symlink` on a dangling link said 0. It now pops, then uninstalls,
  so a nested block's end still leaves the outer one in force.
  `examples/audit-demo.ae` and the `sandbox_in_spec_block` test, which spell
  the four builtins out, had the same order and are fixed too. Found by sae,
  whose file services now run each operation under `enforce`.

## [0.813.0]

### Fixed

- **`*mod.T` is a type, and a qualified type names a module that has it.**
  `mod.T` parsed in a type position, but its pointer form `*mod.T` stopped
  at the `.` ("Expected LEFT_BRACE, got DOT"), so `f() -> *gpu.GpuShader`
  needed a selective `import gpu (GpuShader)` and `*GpuShader`. It now parses
  in a return type, a parameter, a struct field, an `as` cast and a typed
  declaration, as the struct the selective import would bring in. The
  qualifier was also dropped unchecked: `gpu.Missing` reached the C compiler
  as an unknown type name. It is now an error at the source line, `module
  'gpu' has no type 'Missing'`, and so are a qualifier naming no imported
  module and a type the module does not export. `ae fmt` no longer writes a
  line-leading `*Node n = ...` as `* Node n = ...`.

- **INT64_MIN and INT32_MIN emit as C that compiles warning-free.** The
  constant folder turns `(0 - 9223372036854775807) - 1` into the literal
  `-9223372036854775808`, which reached the C as is: `-` applied to a decimal
  that fits no signed type, which clang warns is taken as unsigned and gcc
  as "so large that it is unsigned", both errors under CI's -Werror. Folded
  `(0 - 2147483647) - 1` had the same shape one width down, a `long` that
  `printf("%d", ...)` warned on. Both now emit as `<stdint.h>` spells them,
  `(-9223372036854775807LL - 1)` and `(-2147483647 - 1)`, and so does a
  `@derive(schema)` attribute argument of the minimum.

- **docs/quote.md says what type a lane has in a quote's tree.** It said
  `uv.x * 10.0` was a `float`; the tree says `f32`, as the checker types
  `.x` of any `f32x4` or distinct type over one. `f32` is the honest answer
  (Aether's `float` is a C double, and a lane holds a 32-bit float), so the
  tree stays as it is: docs/quote.md and std/quote's README now say the
  types are Aether's spellings and a GLSL back end maps both `float` and
  `f32` to GLSL's `float`, and `test_quote_fxaa.ae` holds the lane type.

## [0.812.0]

### Fixed

- **Every Valgrind run in CI and the Makefile uses `--fair-sched=yes`
  (#2881).** The massif profiling job ran on Valgrind's default lock, which
  lets a busy-waiting thread keep it while the thread it waits on starves
  (#2593), so the scheduler teardown test took from 4 to 76 s there and now
  and then ran past its 120 s limit and failed main. The CI Valgrind runtime
  suite, `make test-valgrind`, `make valgrind-check` and the contrib Valgrind
  gate take the flag too.

## [0.811.0]

### Fixed

- **A closure's tuple destructure writes outer locals a destructure bound.**
  `a, b = three()` followed by `bump = || { a, b = two() }` left `a` and
  `b` as they were after `bump()`: the lookup of the outer binding a
  closure writes through took a statement for a binding of `a` only when
  it was a single `a = ...`, so the closure's destructure declared locals
  of its own. A tuple destructure is a binding of every name it binds now,
  so the closure writes the outer `int`, `string` or `fn` slots through
  their cells, in a function, in `main`, in a loop body and from a closure
  nested in another (#2762). Each slot that re-binds a local, outer or in
  its own scope, is checked as `a = 7` is: a slot of another kind is the
  "cannot re-bind" error at the slot, a float into an inferred `int` the
  narrowing error, and a value C converts is stored as the local's type.
  Before, such a slot reached the C compiler (`assignment to 'const char *'
  from 'int'`) or truncated silently.

- **A closure passed to a function that hands it back is released.**
  `g2 = keep(g)` over `keep(f: fn) -> fn { return f }`, or
  `g2, m = pair(g)` over `return f, 5`, leaked the closure's environment
  on every call: passing `g` counted as a keep, since the callee returns
  its parameter, so `g` stopped owning its env at the call, and `g2` was
  bound to a value someone else held, so it never started. Such a call is
  now the argument itself: a plain local bound to it, or a tuple slot it
  hands the argument back at, is an alias that retains, as `g2 = g` does
  (#2668), and the argument is judged where the call's value goes, as the
  name would be (a store, a cell, a `_` slot, another call). The same
  holds through a function that returns `keep(f)`, for `return keep(g)` of
  a local, whose caller now owns the closure, and for a closure literal
  passed to a function that binds its parameter so, which the caller now
  releases after the call. The argument is the one at the returned
  parameter's position, where a literal or `_` pattern parameter takes one
  too: `h = sel(0, g, k)` over `sel(0, a, b) { return b }` leaked both
  closures before. `h = keep(o.cb)` retains the field's closure as
  `h = o.cb` does, so replacing `o` no longer leaves `h` calling a freed
  environment (#2763). A closure cell passed to such a call still pins
  what it holds, since the call may rebind the cell; #2788 tracks that.

- **A `return` in a call's trailing block counts as one of the function's
  returns.** The block, `f(x) { ... }`, runs inline, so its `return` returns
  from the function around it, but every pass that asks what a function
  returns stopped at it as at a closure: codegen's `has_return_value`, the
  checker's mirror, the settle of which functions return a value, return-type
  inference and the heap-string return walks. A function with no written
  result type whose only value `return` was in such a block was emitted
  `void` (gcc: "'return' with a value, in function returning void"), and a
  binding of its call was refused ("returns no value"); a closure likewise.
  The block is now part of its function everywhere: the function returns the
  value, typed from it, a path that runs off the end after such a return is
  the missing-return error, the checker checks the `return` against the
  function's result type (a bare enum member there was "Undefined
  variable"), and a bare call returned from a member-access call's block is
  settled through the block's receiver (`return note(n)` in `blk.run() { }`
  is `blk.note`), as the checker resolves it (#2766).

  Such a call is the receiver's function before a function of the program or
  a local of the function of the same name, in every pass alike: beside a
  program's `note(n: int) -> int`, inference typed `return note(n)` by that
  `note`, so the function was declared `int` around the bare `return` the
  checker made of it; the module prune also dropped `blk.note` when a local
  was named `note`. Since a return in a block now gives the function its
  type, some programs behave otherwise than before: a `long` returned from a
  block is no longer cut to an int, and a function with no written type whose
  first `return` gives an int inside a block and a later one `return 2.5` is
  the narrowing error of #2782, as it is with the first `return` outside a
  block (before #2782 both returned 2).

- **The empty literal `[]` in a `T[]` slot is the empty slice.** A slice is
  an AetherSlice struct in C, and the checker turned a `T[N]` array or `null`
  in a slice slot into one, but not `[]`: `let xs: int[] = []` reached C as
  `AetherSlice xs = NULL` ("invalid initializer"), and an argument, a
  `return`, a re-bind or a struct field as `{}`. `[]` is now the empty slice
  wherever a `T[]` is expected, as `null` is: `.len` is 0, it views no
  storage, and it compares equal to `null` (#2767).
- **A module-level `T[]` takes the empty slice.** `var gs: int[] = null` was
  a call in a static initializer ("initializer element is not constant"),
  `const E: int[] = null` or `= []` was emitted as a C array, `var gs:
  int[] = []` was refused as not constant, and `gs = []` in a function
  reached C uncoerced. Each is now the constant empty slice, and a bare
  re-bind of a module-level `T[]` var is checked and coerced against the
  global's type (#2785).

- **A name a `match` arm binds is one variable after the match, as one an
  `if` branch or a `switch` case binds is.** The language reference says a
  name first bound inside a branch and used after it is one variable for the
  whole function, and the shared hoists made that true of `if` and `switch`
  but not of `match`: `match x { 1 -> { v = 10 } _ -> { v = 20 } }` then
  `return v` was "Undefined variable". A match arm's body now joins the same
  hoists, in the checker and in codegen alike: a name read after a match at
  the top of the function body, bound in a `while` body, or bound by every
  arm of a match that runs an arm for every value (a `_` arm, or arms that
  cover its type) is declared ahead of it. A match whose value is used keeps
  its arms' names in the arms, a name an arm's pattern binds (`some(v)`,
  `[h | t]`) is that arm's own and is hoisted out of the match by no rule,
  and any other read after the match is still `Undefined variable` (#2768).
  As in an `if` branch, a closure made in a match arm inside a `while` that
  changes a variable the arm binds now changes the one variable the loop
  declares ahead of it, so closures made on different passes share it (each
  had its own before).
- **A match pattern's variable can be bound again in its arm.** `some(v) ->
  { v = v * 10 }` and `[h | t] -> { h = h * 2 }` failed in the C compiler
  ("redefinition of 'v'"), as did an if/else in the arm binding `v` in both
  branches: codegen declared the binding without recording it, so the arm's
  binding declared it a second time. The binding is now a local of the arm,
  and `v = ...` there rebinds it (#2793).

- **`ae fmt` keeps the space between a keyword and the array literal after
  it.** The formatter wrote no space before a `[` that followed any word
  token, taking it for an index, and a keyword is one: `return []` came out
  as `return[]` and `for x in [1, 2]` as `in[1, 2]`, so `ae fmt --check`
  rejected the spelling the language reference uses. An index follows a
  value (`xs[0]`, `f()[1]`) and `fn[2]` sizes an array type; after any other
  keyword the `[` opens a literal and keeps its space (#2787).

- **A slice of a function's own storage can no longer leave the function.**
  An array literal in a slice slot and a function's own fixed-size array live
  in its frame, so a slice of either that left the function viewed memory
  the next call reused: `gs = [11, 22, 33]` in `fill()`, then any call that
  filled its frame, read `gs[0]` as 0, and a returned slice of a local array
  read garbage the same way. Each way such a slice leaves the function is
  now error E0900 at the value that leaves: a return (alone, in a struct or
  tuple, or in a closure that captured it), a store to a module-level `var`,
  and a store to a field of a struct behind a pointer or of a global. A
  fixed-size array parameter is the function's own copy, so a slice of it
  is refused the same way. What a name holds where it leaves decides: a
  local or a local struct's field re-bound to a `make` buffer before it
  leaves is accepted, one that still holds the frame's storage on any path
  to the exit is not. A re-bind made by a closure call is not counted
  (#2837), and a closure that may store a slice of the frame's storage
  into one of its names gives the name a slice from where it is written
  on (a slice parameter, a `make` buffer, a global or `[]` stored by it
  does not); a closure's store through a pointer is judged as the
  function's. A slice used while the function runs, passed down to
  a call, or of a slice parameter or a `make` buffer, is unchanged (#2785).

- **`[]` is the empty slice in an if-expression or match arm, in a
  comparison and in a C function's `T[]` parameter.** An if-expression or a
  `match` given to a `T[]` was coerced as one value, so a `[]` arm stayed an
  array initializer (gcc: "invalid initializer", "invalid use of void
  expression"), and a `match` of arrays into a slice was not valid C at all.
  Each arm now goes into the slot on its own. `s == []` compared the slice
  with `{}`; the empty slice views no storage, so it is now `s == null`
  (test `s.len == 0` for emptiness). A C function's `T[]` parameter given
  `[]` had `{}` in its call; it now gets the null pointer (#2789).

- **A module-level struct `var` takes `[]` or `null` for a `T[]` field.**
  The field's empty slice was not taken for a constant, so `var g: S = S {
  xs: [], n: 1 }` was refused as not a compile-time constant; it is now the
  constant `{0}` in the struct's static initializer, as for a `T[]` global
  (#2792).

- **`int k = match n { ... }` binds the match's value.** The C-style typed
  declaration parsed its initializer as an expression, and `match` is none,
  so `k` was declared with no value and the match ran as the next statement
  with its values dropped: `k` read whatever the stack held. It now takes
  the match as its value, as `k = match` and `let k: int = match` do
  (#2790).

- **Leaving a builder's trailing block early releases the builder's
  config.** A builder call makes its config with the builder's factory, runs
  the block against it and hands it to the builder, which owns it from then
  on. A `return` in the block, with a value or without, or a `break` or
  `continue` out of it, left before the builder ran, and nothing released
  the config: every such call leaked it (a `map_new` config with one option
  set, 260 bytes a call). Any way out of the block but its natural end now
  releases it, with `map_free` for the default `map_new` and with
  `<stem>_free` for a `<stem>_new` factory the program defines or declares
  (`list_new`, `list_free`); a nested builder call's block releases both
  calls' configs. A factory without such a release still leaves its config
  to the builder's protocol (#2791).

- **A builder with the default config factory builds without `import
  std.map`.** Its calls are lowered to `map_new()`, which nothing declared
  unless the program imported std.map, so a program whose builder never
  touched its config failed in the C compiler ("implicit declaration of
  function 'map_new'"). The generated C now declares `map_new` and
  `map_free` whenever a builder uses the default factory (#2801).

- **A returned value is checked against the result type.** The checker
  checked what a `return` gives on its own and never asked whether it fits
  the result type, as it asks of a typed binding's value, so every mismatch
  reached the C compiler: `word(n: int) -> string { return n }` failed with
  "returning 'int' from a function with return type 'const char *'". A
  value of another kind is now E0200 at the `return`, naming both types, in
  a function, a closure and a call's trailing block, value by value in a
  multi-value return and arm by arm in an `if` or `match` returned for its
  value. The rules are a typed binding's, with what C converts: numeric
  scalars into one another, a bool to an integer and back, `T` to `T?`,
  `none`, a variant to its sum, an enum to an integer and back, `null` or an
  int to a pointer, `null` or `[]` to a slice, and a C string pointer to a
  `string` and back. With no result type written, the first `return`'s type
  is the result, and a later `return` an inferred `int` would truncate (a
  `long`, a `uint32`, a `float`) is the narrowing error an inferred `int`
  local gives. Some returns that compiled before are refused, because the
  value was converted to something it does not mean: an enum returned as a
  `string`, a pointer, a float, a byte or a bool, a bool returned as a float,
  a pointer or an enum, a pointer or a float returned as a bool, a float or
  a byte returned as an enum, a number, a bool, an enum or a typed pointer
  returned as a `string?`, and `[]` returned as an `int?`. A closure
  returned as a `ptr`, a pointer returned as a closure or a value optional,
  and `[]` returned as a scalar failed in the C compiler before and are
  refused with the fix (`box_closure`, `unbox_closure`, `none`) (#2782).

- **A `match` bound to an optional takes each arm's value wrapped.**
  `int? o = match n { 1 -> 41  _ -> none }`, its `let o: int? = match`
  form, a `string?` or a struct's optional bound the same way, a re-bind
  `o = match ...` and a `match` returned from a `-> T?` function emitted
  the whole match as one expression inside the optional's wrap (gcc:
  "'n141_' undeclared", "incompatible types when assigning to type
  'ae_opt_int'"). The match is now bound arm by arm, as a match of any
  other type is, each arm's value wrapped into the optional and `none` the
  empty one; a `string?` local owns the arm's string when it is a fresh
  one, as a single-value binding decides (#2816).

- **A panic out of a builder block, or after a string went into a map, no
  longer corrupts the heap when a `try` catches it.** Two faults met in
  `try { run("x") { set_opt("k", "v")  boom(1) } } catch e { }`, which
  crashed with heap corruption within a few hundred catches. The panic
  leaves the block by longjmp, skipping the block's context pop and the
  config release of #2791: every caught panic left an entry on the builder
  context stack, and after 64 of them a block's setters filled the config
  of a call a panic had abandoned. The catch now puts the stack back to its
  depth at the `try` and releases the configs of the blocks the panic
  abandoned. And a string a setter passed on to `map.put` (or `list.add`)
  was adopted by the container while still in the panic journal its first
  owner kept it in, so the panic's drain freed it under the container and
  freeing the container freed it again; a plain map filled in a `try` body
  crashed the same way. A container that adopts a string now takes it out
  of the journal (#2810).

- **A function whose result type is a struct's optional parses.**
  `find(n: int) -> Point? { ... }` was "Expected IDENTIFIER, got
  LEFT_BRACE": the definition parser read `-> Name` as a written result
  type only when `{` followed the name (or a bracket group and then `{`),
  so the `?` sent it to the arrow-body path and left the body over. A `?`
  between the name and the body, or a `requires` / `ensures` clause, now
  marks a result type as it does after a qualified name (#2809).

- **An enum converts to and from a `byte` as it does a `uint8`.** A `byte`
  is C's `uint8_t`, as `uint8` is, but the enum rule took only the integer
  scalars, which leave `byte` out: `let x: byte = Color.Green` and `let c:
  Color = b` were "Type mismatch in variable initialization", and with the
  return check of #2782 so were `-> byte { return Color.Blue }`, `-> Color {
  return b }` and a `(byte, int)` result, while the same programs with
  `uint8` compiled. A byte-coded enum (a wire format) now binds, passes and
  returns as a byte and back (#2782).

- **A variant put into a sum's optional is wrapped into the sum.** Returned
  from a `-> Shape?` function, bound to a `Shape?` local or passed to a
  `Shape?` parameter, a `Circle { ... }` was written as the optional's value
  as it was, and the C compiler refused it ("incompatible types when
  initializing type 'enum <anonymous>' using type 'Circle'"). The optional's
  wrap now wraps a variant into the sum first, as a variant into the sum
  itself is (#2826).

- **`Point? q = ...` declares a struct's optional.** The C-style typed
  declaration took `Point p`, `Pair[8] ps` and `mod.Type t` as declarations,
  but not a struct's optional: `Point? q = match n { ... }` and `Point? r =
  Point { x: 7 }` were "unexpected `?` in expression", the `?` read as the
  ask operator. A name, `?`, a second name and `=` on one line now declare
  one. Without the `=` the line is still an ask, as `d ? GetCount` is (an
  ask whose message has no braces, or has them on the next line), whatever
  the first name also names; a struct's optional with no value is spelled
  `let r: Point? = none` (#2827).

- **A variant or a bare value reaches a sum or an optional everywhere it is
  given one.** Three places passed it as it was, and the C compiler refused
  the result: a variant as the default of `??` over a `Shape?` (`e ?? Circle
  { r: 1.0 }`, "type mismatch in conditional expression", #2839), and the
  arguments of a closure call, `call(f, Circle { ... })` into `|s: Shape|`
  or `|o: Shape?|` and `call(h, 3)` or `call(h, none)` into `|o: int?|`
  ("incompatible type for argument 2", #2840). Each is now wrapped as a
  direct call's argument is. And `c2 = o2`, after `o2 = Circle { ... }` on a
  `Shape?` local, was "Type mismatch in variable initialization": the early
  pass took `c2` for the Circle last put in `o2`. The first binding of a
  name with no written type now takes the optional or sum it is given
  (#2841). A field read plainly off an optional (`c2.r`, `o2.r`, `p.x` on
  a `Point?`) was accepted and failed in C ("'ae_opt_Shape' has no member
  named 'r'"); it is now a type error naming `?.`, `!` and narrowing.

- **`none` and `[]` through a bare `fn` are refused, not guessed.** Since
  #2840 a closure call wraps an argument into the parameter's optional or
  sum when the closure's parameter types are known. Through an erased call
  (`apply_none(f: fn) -> int { return call(f, none) }`) they are not, and
  the argument's own type stood in for them: `none` was built as an int
  optional ("unresolved type in codegen, defaulting to int"), and given to
  `|o: string?|` or `|o: Big?|` the program crashed. `none` and `[]` given
  through a bare `fn`, as `call(f, none)` or `f(none)`, are now an error
  at the argument; bind the value to a local of the parameter's type and
  pass that. Arguments are coerced only into parameter types a signature
  or the closure literal gives (#2840).

- **The C a program gets for a compiler that is not GCC-compatible has no
  GNU statement expressions.** Every construct that needs a temporary in the
  middle of an expression wrote `({ ... })` whatever the C compiler, so on
  the path `AETHER_GCC_COMPAT 0` selects, which is what cl.exe compiles, 445
  of the 971 programs of the .ae sweep did not compile: storing a string into
  an array element, an argument freed after its call, an operand evaluated
  ahead to keep source order (which also used `__auto_type`), and the
  `!`, `??`, `?.`, `or` and string ownership forms among them. Each is now a
  comma expression whose temporaries are declared ahead of the statement it
  is in, the same C for every compiler; an evaluation-order temporary keeps
  `__auto_type` where the compiler has it and is declared with the
  operand's type where it does not. An `or` with a block handler, a `!` that
  propagates an error and a call whose trailing block runs where its value
  is used run as statements ahead of their statement when they are the
  first thing it evaluates (anywhere else too since #2798). Every program
  of the sweep the compiler translates (975 of 977)
  now compiles as strict C11 with `AETHER_GCC_COMPAT 0` and runs right that
  way under gcc; under cl.exe 933 compile, the rest on other GCC-isms
  (#2799). `make test-msvc-compat` compiles a program per construct as
  strict C11 and under cl.exe, and runs them that way (#2765).

- **A tuple destructure into an optional local compiles.** `let a: int? =
  none` then `a, b = two()`, or the `string?` equivalent, stored the
  slot's bare value into the `ae_opt_<T>` variable, and gcc rejected the
  C. The slot is wrapped now, as `a = 7` wraps a value, and a `string?`
  local frees the string it held and owns the new one when the call handed
  it over. The same holds for a closure's destructure that writes an outer
  optional (#2794).

- **An optional a closure writes is a cell.** `let a: int? = 3` followed by
  `set = || { a = 5 }` did not compile: the optional declaration path
  declared and stored a plain `ae_opt_int`, so the closure's capture of
  the cell was handed a value. The first binding makes the cell now and
  every store goes through it, a bare value wrapped, whether by `a = v` or
  a destructure slot. A `string?` cell owns its string, as a string cell
  does: a store takes a string of its own and gives back the one it held,
  a `string?` parameter's cell takes one of its own on entry, and the
  cell's last release gives back the last. What a local takes out of it
  (`v = a ?? ""`, `v = a!`, a `some(v)` binding) is a copy of its own, as
  what it takes out of a string cell is, so it outlives the next store
  (#2795).

- **A tuple destructure writes a module-level `var`.** `gx, n = two()` in a
  function declared a local `gx` and left the global as it was, where a
  bare `gx = 7` writes it. The slot writes the global now, taking the value
  as a global takes one: a string of its own, and a reference of its own
  to a closure, giving back the one it held. A local or parameter of the
  same name still shadows the global (#2796).

- **A closure can store a string into an outer `ptr` local.** `q, n =
  names(p)` or `r = s` in a closure, where `q` and `r` are `ptr` locals the
  closure writes, handed the `ptr` cell to the string cell setter, and gcc
  rejected the C. The store follows the cell's type now, and a string
  stored into a `ptr` cell reaches C as its characters, as a plain string
  stored by the cell's own scope does: the cell keeps a string of its own
  beside the pointer until the next string store or its last release, so
  the characters outlive the closure that stored them (#2797).

- **A module-level optional `var` can be declared.** `var g: int? = 3` gave
  the file-scope static its value bare, an invalid initialiser for the
  `ae_opt_int` struct; `= none` was refused as not a constant, a struct
  literal was refused for a struct optional, and the constant folder
  re-typed a `string?` with a string value as a plain `string`. The static
  now takes the optional's own constant (`{ .has = 1, .val = 3 }`, `{0}`
  for `none`), and no initialiser means `none`. A function's `g = v`, or a
  tuple destructure slot, writes the global with a bare value wrapped,
  including in a loop body or a closure. A `string?` var takes a string of
  its own and keeps every string it was given, as a `string` var does, so
  whatever reads it (`v = g ?? ""`, `g!`, a `some(v)` binding, a view
  beside a call that re-binds it) stays valid (#2800).

- **`int r = match o { ... }` binds the match's value.** The `T name =
  expr` declaration parsed its initialiser as an expression, which does
  not include `match`, so the declaration had no initialiser and the match
  ran as a statement of its own: `r` was read uninitialised. It parses the
  match as `let r: int = match ...` does (#2803).

- **A closure writes a module-level `var` itself.** A closure that wrote a
  module `var` (`set = || { gnum = 11 }`) turned the name into a cell of
  the enclosing function's own, for the whole function: neither the
  closure's stores nor the function's own `gnum = 9` reached the global,
  so the function saw one value and every other function the old one. A
  closure that read one took a copy. A module `var` is never captured now:
  the closure reads and writes the global, and only a parameter of the
  same name, which shadows it, is captured (#2805).

- **A tuple destructure in a receive arm writes actor state.** `label, seen
  = pair(tag)`, where `label` and `seen` are state fields, declared handler
  locals of those names, so the state kept its old values. The slots now
  write the state, as `label = v` does: a string field takes a string of
  its own and gives back the one it held, a `fn` field a reference of its
  own, and an optional field takes the slot as the optional (#2806).

- **A `const` can have an optional type.** `const LIMIT: int? = 3` gave its
  `static const ae_opt_int` the bare value, which gcc rejected, and `const
  NO_LABEL: string? = none` was refused as not a constant. The constant
  takes the optional's own value now (`{ .has = 1, .val = 3 }`, `{0}` for
  `none`) and reads, `??` and `match` work on it (#2807).

- **A string stored into a module-level `ptr` var builds without a C
  warning.** `gp = s` or `gp = string.concat(...)`, with `gp` a `ptr`
  global, assigned a `const char*` to the `void*` static, and gcc warned
  (discards 'const' qualifier) in the user's build, an error under
  `-Werror`. The store casts to the global's type (#2811).

- **Every operand a later call can write is read before the call, as
  written.** In `println("${flag} ${gc == Color.Green} ${gb} ${gu}
  ${step()}")`, where `step()` rewrites all four module globals, the `bool`
  and the enum comparison printed their values from before `step()` but the
  `byte` and the `uint16` printed what it wrote (`true true 7 8 9` for
  `true true 1 2 9`): an interpolation segment of a type narrower than
  `int` (a `byte`, `uint8`, `uint16`, enum, bitstruct or bit set) had no
  temporary type, so it was left in place and read wherever the C compiler
  evaluated it. And a struct field read through a pointer, before a call
  that writes that field through a pointer of its own (a global pointer, a
  parameter), was read after the call in an argument list, a literal or an
  operation: what a function writes through a pointer did not count among
  what its call can change. Both are now evaluated ahead of the call, on
  the GCC path and without GCC extensions. So is a call that reads through
  a pointer it was not handed (one in a module variable, one inside a
  struct it was handed) against a call that writes through one, in either
  order; and what functions read and write is solved over the call graph,
  so mutually recursive ones answer the same whichever is asked about
  first (#2813).

- **An `or` with a block, a propagating `!` and a trailing-block call are
  plain C wherever they are.** On the path `AETHER_GCC_COMPAT 0` selects
  (what cl.exe compiles), these constructs, which run statements, were GNU
  statement expressions anywhere but the first thing their statement
  evaluates: after another operand (`y + (f() or { -1 })`, a second
  argument), in a loop condition, behind `&&` or `||`, in a branch of an
  `if` expression or the default of `??`, in a compound assignment, a
  struct literal's field, a `for` loop's init or increment, a `match` arm's
  value, an actor state's initializer, and in a statement that keeps the
  structs its calls return in temporaries. Each now runs as statements
  ahead of its statement, after whatever the statement evaluates before
  it, which is evaluated into temporaries first, in source order; one in a
  conditional part runs under the same test, and one in a loop condition at
  the top of every pass. A builder's arguments are evaluated after its
  block, left to right, whether the call is a value or a statement of its
  own; as a value, an argument holding one of these constructs ran before
  the block. Nothing in the .ae sweep, or in programs written to reach each
  of these places, is a statement expression on that path any more
  (#2798).

- **A thrown-away string made from a field of a struct a call returns no
  longer leaks the struct.** `string.concat(item(2).label, "e")` on a line
  of its own freed the string it made but never destroyed the struct
  `item(2)` returned, so that struct's strings leaked once per statement;
  the statement now keeps such structs in temporaries and destroys them, as
  it already did for any other value it throws away (#2817).

- **An actor state initialized by an `or` has the type of its value.** The
  typechecker took the type of a state's initializer only when it was a
  plain call, so `state name = word(true, "q") or { "dflt" }` left the field
  untyped: codegen declared it `int`, and the program did not compile (a
  string assigned to an int, an int passed to `string.length`). An int
  field compiled, with warnings, but its uses in the handlers were untyped.
  Such a field now has the type its initializer infers to (#2821).

- **An `if` expression used as an operand has its own value.** It was
  written as a C conditional with no parentheses around it, and `?:` binds
  looser than any operator, so `y + (if c { 10 } else { 20 })` computed
  `(y + c) ? 10 : 20` and `(if c { 10 } else { 20 }) * 2` doubled the
  else branch only. The conditional is now parenthesised whole (#2824).

- **A struct can hold an optional field.** `struct Box { v: int? }` named
  `ae_opt_int` before its typedef, which came after every struct body, and
  `Box { v: 7 }` or `b.v = none` gave the field a bare value, so gcc
  rejected the program. The typedef a struct needs is declared ahead of
  it (an optional of a struct after that struct's body), and a literal or
  a field store wraps a bare value as an optional binding does. An
  optional field whose value owns memory (`string?`, an optional `fn`, an
  optional of a struct, a fixed-size array or a tuple holding a string or
  a closure) is refused with a diagnostic until it has a `string` field's
  ownership (#2820, #2822).

- **Returning a `some(s)` binding no longer leaks.** In a function that
  matched a `string?` call result (or a `string?` closure cell of its own)
  and returned the `some(s)` binding beside a literal, `return s` handed
  over the binding's own string, but the function was classified as
  returning borrowed strings, so the caller never freed it: 37 bytes a
  call. The binding counts as a heap return now, and the literal beside
  it is copied (#2823).

- **Returning `w ?? d` or `w!` from a `string?` local no longer returns
  freed memory.** The return read the string out of the local, the
  local's scope-exit free gave it back, and the caller got the freed
  pointer, which printed other strings' bytes once the block was reused.
  The function is heap-returning for such a return now and hands the
  caller a copy, the local freeing its own; a fresh default is handed
  over as it is. A tuple position does the same (#2815).

- **A tuple literal can become an optional.** `let t: (int, int)? = (3, 4)`
  stored `34` (its elements' text run together) and printed `34 0`, the
  same in an `(int, int)?` struct field's literal or store, and `(s, 1)`
  became the undeclared name `s1`. The literal is the tuple's compound
  literal inside the optional now, each element cast to its slot's type
  (#2833).

- **Returning `w ?? d` no longer frees `d` first.** With `d` a parameter
  the function captures (it escapes through that return) or a local bound
  to a heap string, `return w ?? d` read `d`, then the scope-exit free gave
  it back and the caller got the freed pointer. Such a return makes the
  function heap-returning now, and the value taken is copied (#2834).

- **Returning the `some(s)` binding of a `string?` local no longer returns
  freed memory.** The binding was a view of the local's string, which the
  local freed at scope exit before the caller read it, through `return s`
  or a tuple's `return s, 1`. The binding is a copy the arm owns now, as
  over a closure cell, and both returns hand it over; an owned binding at
  a tuple position counts as a heap return as it does at a single one
  (#2835).

- **A struct's string field handed to a function that keeps it stays
  alive.** A function that stores its `string` parameter where nothing
  releases it (a module-level `var`, say) keeps the pointer it was given;
  a local handed to one is not freed at its scope exit, but a struct field
  was freed by the struct's destructor, at once for a struct a call
  returned: `n = string.length(keep(make_item(w).name))` left the kept
  string pointing at freed memory. The field now gives its reference up at
  the call, as it does to a function that frees it (#2843).

- **A fallible function's built error string is freed.** A `T!` function
  that returns a bare value on success and builds its error on another path
  (`return "", string.concat("bad-", w)`) had the error position of its
  result taken for an unfreeable passthrough, so the `or`, the destructure
  and `_, _ =` that discarded the error never freed it. The position is now
  heap whenever a return builds its error, and the success sentinel is a
  string the caller owns as well. `x!` reads the error slot as the `or` does
  (an owned empty slot read raw looked like an error, so `x!` panicked on
  success), frees the sentinel on success, and a propagating `x!` copies a
  literal error it hands on into a position the caller frees (#2863).
- **`x!` in main() compiles after a `T!` function.** The function emitted
  before main left its result type in place, and main's `x!` was lowered as
  a propagation returning the result tuple from `main` (#2864).
- **A tuple's heap strings are freed when nothing binds them.** A tuple call
  thrown away as a statement (`pair(w)`), and `f()!` over a tuple whose first
  slot is a heap string used in place (`pair(w)! == x`), left the strings to
  nobody (#2865).

- **A builder call with a trailing block is stored, passed and thrown away
  as any call is.** Its statement forms assigned `s = label(args, cfg)` by
  hand after the block, so a string it returned was never tracked (bound to
  a local, replaced, or thrown away, it leaked, #2866), a fresh string passed
  to it was never freed (#2853), a string field passed to one that frees or
  keeps its parameter was not handed over (#2851), and stored into a struct
  field it ran with its block dropped (#2855). The block and the arguments
  now run ahead of the statement, which is then emitted as for any value,
  the call made with the filled config.

- **Passing a parameter on to a `string?` tuple position copies nothing
  extra.** A named function hands its `string?` tuple positions over owned,
  a copy, but the keep analysis took them for keeping the parameter, so a
  function that passed its parameter to one copied it on entry and leaked
  the copy; and a returned tuple local holding such a call's result was
  copied, its own string leaked (#2867).

- **An `fn[N]` local releases its closures.** A local array built from
  capturing closure literals held the one reference to each environment and
  never released them, so each call of a function holding one leaked them
  all. Its scope exit now releases them, as a closure local's does; a struct
  given the array takes references of its own (#2868).

- **Mutually recursive functions agree on what they hand over.** A return
  classifier answers no for a function it is still classifying, and a
  function classified from that answer kept it, so of two tuple functions
  calling each other one could hand an error string the other built over as
  borrowed, and every caller leaked it (std.message's `parse` on a bad
  pattern). An answer that rested on such a no is now kept only while the
  function it rested on is being classified (#2870).

## [0.810.0]

### Added

- **`quote`: a trailing block handed to the function as a tree.**
  `f(args) quote | a: T | { body }` (also `quote | a: T | -> expr`,
  `quote { body }`, `quote -> expr`) is a fourth trailing-block form beside
  the immediate block, the closure and `callback`. The block is
  type-checked as Aether but never runs: the function, whose last
  parameter is a `quote.Tree`, receives a tree describing it, every node
  carrying the type the checker gave it (a `vec2` declared
  `distinct f32x4` stays `vec2`), each call recorded with its name as
  written rather than made, and each enclosing variable the block reads a
  capture whose cell is the variable itself, so a change the program makes
  after the tree is built is seen through it (a program-level `var` is a
  capture too, its cell the global itself). That is what a shader
  library needs to write GLSL with its uniforms found for it, and what a
  query builder or a test library that prints the failing expression
  needs. The new `std.quote` module reads the tree (kinds, accessors,
  `children` and a pre-order `walk` taking a closure,
  typed capture getters that panic naming both types on a mismatch, a
  printer back to Aether source, a typed dump, a hash of the tree's shape
  for caching). `quote` is not a keyword: it quotes only straight after a
  call's `)` on the same line. Version 1 of the tree holds a subset of
  Aether; the rest is rejected at its line, naming the construct (E0800),
  as are an untyped quote parameter (E0801), a quote given where no
  `quote.Tree` is taken or a closure where one is (E0802), and a write to
  or the address of a captured variable (E0803). See docs/quote.md.

## [0.809.0]

### Fixed

- **`make contrib` replaces each archive in one step.** It wrote objects,
  archives and the manifest in place in `build/contrib`, so a link against
  `build/contrib` while it ran could read an archive half rewritten, two
  runs at once overwrote each other's files, and a link that fell between
  the vendored SQLite veneer and the `libsqlite3.a` it calls into got the
  system library instead; on macOS, whose system library has no
  `sqlite3_enable_load_extension`, that failed the link, and the 0.807.0
  and 0.808.0 macOS release builds with it, so neither release was
  published. Each run now builds in a directory of its own and moves every
  archive into place with a rename, the vendored `libsqlite3.a` before the
  veneer that needs it and the manifest last. `CONTRIB_OUT` builds into
  another directory (#2780).

## [0.808.0]

### Fixed

- **A scalar variable beside a lane value splats, as a literal does.** The
  language reference says a scalar operand splats, and the type checker
  accepted `v * s` for an `f32x4` `v` and a `float` `s`, but the generated
  `v * s` put a C `double` beside a vector of `float`, which clang and GCC
  reject ("implicit conversion would cause truncation"); only a literal,
  being a constant, compiled. The scalar is now converted to the lane's
  element type before C broadcasts it, for `f32x4`, `f64x2`, `i32x4`,
  `i64x2` and `i16x8` (`f32x8` / `i32x8` already splatted through their
  helpers), for every arithmetic and comparison operator, with the scalar on
  either side, in a compound assignment (`v *= s`), and through a distinct
  type over a lane type (`type vec4 = distinct f32x4`).

- **An operator does not mix two different distinct types.** Distinct types
  have nominal identity, enforced at assignments and call arguments, but
  `USD + EUR` (both `distinct float`) compiled and added the two, as did
  `vec3 + vec4` over the same lane type. A binary operator, comparison or
  compound assignment whose operands are two different distinct types is now
  a type error (E0200) naming both: `'+' mixes distinct types USD and EUR`.
  The same distinct type on both sides now keeps it (`USD + USD` is a `USD`,
  so `usd += usd` and passing the sum where a `USD` is wanted work without a
  cast; before, the result was the base `float`), and a distinct lane type
  scaled by a scalar keeps it (`vec4 * s` is a `vec4`). A distinct type
  beside a plain value of its base (`USD + 1.0`) is unchanged: computed over
  the base, the result is the base. See docs/distinct-types.md.

## [0.807.0]

### Changed

- **The language reference lists every `match` pattern.** Match Expressions
  named only integer and string literals, `_` and list patterns. It now lists
  each kind (literals, a variable or constant name, ranges, comma-lists,
  `_`, enum members, sum variants, `none` / `some(v)` and list patterns),
  what it matches and over what, with runnable examples, and the errors an
  arm the value cannot match gives (#2730).

### Fixed

- **std.http's server answers a request line that is not HTTP with 400 and
  closes the connection.** `THIS IS NOT HTTP` was taken for a request (method
  `THIS`, path `IS`), answered 404, and the connection kept open for a next
  request the client never sends, so the client sat on it until its own
  timeout. A request line whose version is not `HTTP/1.0` or `HTTP/1.1`, and
  any request that does not parse, is now answered `400 Bad Request` with
  `Connection: close` (#2760).

- **`ae test a.ae b.ae` runs both files.** Every argument that was not a flag
  was assigned to one target and only that one was collected, so the second
  file was dropped without a word and a failing test in it passed the run.
  Every file and directory named now runs, in the order given, and the run
  fails if any test in any of them fails. A target that is neither a file nor
  a directory is an error naming it; it used to fall back to running
  `tests/`, so a mistyped name ran something else and could pass (#2752).

- **`ae <command> --help` prints the command's options and does nothing
  else.** Inside a project `ae build --help` built the project: the build
  skipped the flag as consumed by an earlier parse that had never acted on
  it. Most commands had the same fault in some form: `run`, `check`,
  `inspect`, `test` and `examples` ran or built, `install` and `upgrade` went
  to the network, `repl` started, `use` and `lib-info` took `--help` for a
  name, and `init`, `add`, `cache` and `bindgen` printed their usage as an
  error. `-h` and `--help` are now answered before any command runs, for
  every command, with its usage on stdout and exit code 0; after `--`, as in
  `ae run app.ae -- --help`, they still go to the program. `ae help` lists
  `lib-info` too (#2753).

- **A hung test on Windows ends as `[TIMEOUT]` without signalling anything.**
  The sweep's time limits were `timeout(1)`, which ends a hung test by
  signalling its process group; on Windows a signal to the MSYS2 process
  standing in for a native program makes the MSYS2 runtime signal unrelated
  processes found through recycled parent pids, the CI step's own `bash`
  among them, and a SIGTERM injects an exit into any native process it
  reaches. On Windows the limits of `run_ae_test.sh`, `run_ae_sh_dir.sh`,
  `run_stage.sh` (and the `-O0`/`-O2` comparison and `make examples-run`) are
  now a job object around the test, which a small native watchdog
  (`tests/lib/sweep_watchdog.c`) ends with TerminateJobObject: the test and
  everything it started go, nothing else is touched, and the result is the
  same 124 (#2758). Linux keeps `timeout(1)`.

- **HTTPS on Windows trusts the system certificate store, and both TLS stacks
  agree on what they trust.** Neither `std.http.client` over OpenSSL nor the
  pure-Aether `std.cryptography.tls13_client` read the Windows store, so a
  program copied to a machine without MSYS2 or Git for Windows could make no
  HTTPS request, and the two looked for different bundle files, so one could
  work where the other failed. Both now trust, unless `SSL_CERT_FILE` or
  `SSL_CERT_DIR` is set, every certificate of the ROOT system store together
  with the first bundle of one shared list: the bundle the release ships
  beside the program, MSYS2's MINGW64 and UCRT64 bundles, then Git for
  Windows'. An `SSL_CERT_FILE` that cannot be read now fails closed on the
  OpenSSL stack too, as it did on the pure one, instead of falling back to
  the bundle files (#2675).

- **The C written for non-GCC compilers is checked in CI, by cl.exe itself.**
  `tests/compiler/test_msvc_compat.sh`, which compiles generated C with
  `AETHER_GCC_COMPAT 0` (the path MSVC takes), was run by no target or
  workflow, and needed `python3`, which MSYS2 lacks. It now runs as strict C11
  under gcc on the Linux / GCC leg and under cl.exe in the Windows workflow's
  MSVC job, where the warnings that mean a C type error (an undeclared
  function, a wrong argument type, a dropped qualifier) fail it; it gained a
  closure over arrays a `try` body writes, the case of #2691. `make
  test-msvc-compat` runs it locally (#2725). A string stored into an array
  element is still a GNU statement expression on that path, which cl.exe
  cannot compile (#2765).

- **A `match` arm and a `switch` case are checked against the value they
  compare.** Nothing checked an arm's pattern against the value matched, so
  the C compiler met the mistakes: an arm naming no variable (`other ->`) was
  "'other' undeclared" at a misplaced line, a string arm over an `int`
  compared a pointer with an integer and never ran, a literal arm over an
  optional or a sum was dropped without a word, and `none`, `some(v)`, a list
  pattern or a range over a value they cannot match failed in C. Each is now
  an error at the arm, saying what the arm compares and how to write it, and
  a `switch` case is checked the same way. A comma-list of bare enum members
  (`Red, Green ->`) and a bare member in a `switch` case now name the
  members, where they were undeclared names in C; a `switch` over a string or
  a float compares by content or value, where it was a C `switch` on a
  pointer; and a `uint64` or `uint32` value is matched as itself, where it was
  cut to an `int` (5000000000 took the arm for 705032704) (#2727).

- **A receive arm frees the strings its locals hold.** A string a receive
  arm built into a local (`msg = string.concat(w, "!")`) was never freed:
  the handler declared the local's ownership flag but ran neither the
  escape walk nor the exit frees a function body gets, so every message
  that ran the arm leaked the string, and a pattern binding rebound to a
  heap string (`w = string.concat(w, x)`) leaked the same way. A `string?`
  or `*StringSeq` local of an arm was not tracked at all. An arm, and the
  `after` arm of a `receive`, now run the same passes as a function body.
  A store of such a local into a string state field (`label = msg`) gives
  the state a string of its own: the local's buffer on the local's last
  use (its flag cleared), a copy otherwise. The state used to take the
  pointer while the local kept its flag set, and two state fields stored
  from one local both owned the same buffer, which was freed twice
  (#2748).

- **W1004 reports a second arm for an enum member, a variant or `none`.**
  `Color.Red ->` twice, `Red ->` twice or one of each in one `match` was not
  reported as unreachable: the member had been lowered to its constant
  before the arms were compared, and only literal arms were compared. Over an
  enum, a sum or an optional, where the cases are known, every arm is now
  compared, and a comma-list arm is reported when earlier arms name all its
  values. The arm that runs is the first, as reported: a repeated variant arm
  made a second C `case` for the same value, which the C compiler refused,
  and a repeated `none` arm, or one after `_`, took the first one's place.
  The string literal `"_"` is a string, not the wildcard: an arm for it is
  compared, where it was taken for `_` and failed in C (#2728).

- **The effect-tag error names a module's function as the source does.** An
  `@pure` (or `@no_os`, ...) function of an imported module reaching a
  disallowed call was named by its merged C name, `checks_shell`, instead of
  `checks.shell`. It and the always-false `requires` error now name it as a
  caller writes it, through the helper the missing-return error used (#2729).

- **A name first bound in a `switch` case and read after the switch is one
  variable, as one bound in an `if` branch is.** The type checker took the
  cases for part of the enclosing scope, so `switch x { case 1: v = 10 ...
  }` then `return v` passed it and failed in the C compiler ("'v'
  undeclared"), since each case is a C block of its own. Each case is now a
  scope of its own in the checker too, and the rules that let an `if`
  branch's binding outlive the `if` apply to a switch's cases: read after a
  switch at the top of the function body, bound in a `while` body, or bound
  by every case of a switch with a `default`, it is declared ahead; any other
  read after the switch is `Undefined variable` (#2732).

- **A `match` whose value is used, with an arm that calls a function
  returning nothing, is an error at that arm.** The `match` takes its value
  from the arm that runs, and codegen stored the call's void in the result:
  the C compiler stopped with "void value not ignored". A `match` that is
  returned for its value, bound, or the value of an arm of such a `match`
  now refuses the arm, naming the call and how to give the arm a value. An
  arm that ends in a statement, such as a `return`, is accepted as before
  (#2743).

- **Whether a function returns a value is settled right for a tail called
  on a receiver or through a parameter.** The settle that decides, before any
  body is checked, which functions return a value (#2736) resolved the calls
  in their returns by name, so a tail whose callee depends on what it is
  called on was taken to give a value: a UFCS call (`b.show()`,
  `mk(n).show()`), a call through a function-pointer field (`o.run(n)`) and a
  call through a parameter typed `fn(int)` (`f(x)`). The function was emitted
  as returning nothing while its caller returned its value, and the C
  compiler stopped ("void value not ignored"), in either definition order.
  The settle now runs after inference and resolves those calls as the
  checker does, with the receiver's type. Also, `call(f, x)` through a typed
  function pointer is the call `f(x)`, where it was emitted as a closure call
  that C refused (#2744).

- **A loop's local bound by an if-expression or a closure call, read before
  its binding, has the binding's type.** The inference pass that types a
  loop's locals before the checker declares them ahead of the loop typed
  neither an if-expression nor a call through a local bound to a closure
  literal, so `out = "${out}${prev}"` ahead of `prev = if i > 0 { "x" } else
  { "y" }` (or `prev = call(f)` with `f = || -> "z"`) printed pointer values
  as ints. It now types an if-expression by its arms, as the checker does,
  and a call of a closure literal, directly or through a local every binding
  of which is such a literal, by what the literal returns (#2745).

- **A struct literal passed straight to a call is destroyed after it.** A
  function or closure borrows a struct parameter (it disowns the copy's
  strings on entry, or takes references of its own when it keeps the
  value), so `reader(Item { name: string.concat(w, "old") })` left the
  literal's strings to the caller, and nothing destroyed them: every call
  leaked them, while the same literal bound to a local first was
  destroyed at the local's scope exit. Such a literal is now a temporary
  of its statement, as a struct a call returns is (#2582), destroyed once
  the statement is done, nested literals and closure calls included; a
  string the callee hands back from it is copied where the call is made,
  so it outlives the literal (#2749).

- **A `string?` in a tuple a function returns is its caller's own.** A
  fresh string returned in a `string?` position (`return
  string.concat(w, "x"), 1`) leaked on every call: the destructure
  `a, n = two(w)` took it with the local's ownership flag left 0. Each
  `string?` position of a named function's or a closure's tuple now hands
  over a string of its own, as a single `string?` result does (#2740): a
  fresh one or an owning local's as it is, a parameter, a literal or a
  field copied, `none` as nothing; a whole tuple passed on from a C
  function or a closure the compiler cannot name is copied the same way.
  The destructured local owns it and frees the string it replaces, a `_`
  slot frees it at once, and a `string?` parameter a tuple return copies
  no longer keeps its caller's argument (#2751).

- **A closure returned in a tuple is released by the local it lands in.**
  `f, k = pair(piece)` over `return || { ... }, 1` never released the
  closure's env: the destructure took the slot as a plain value, and the
  tuple position was never asked whether the function hands its closure
  over, so every call leaked the env. A position now hands its closure
  over when every return puts there a closure literal, a call that hands
  one over, a local nobody else keeps, or the same position of a tuple
  call passed on, as a single closure result does (#2494). The
  destructured local releases it at its scope exit, a rebinding releases
  the one it replaces, a closure cell gives the slot's reference back
  once it has taken its own, and a `_` slot gives it back at once. A
  closure the callee only lends (a field it read, a parameter it hands
  back) is left to its owner (#2756).

- **A `return` from a block whose string shadows a local frees both.** A
  C-style `for` loop's string variable (#2742), an owning `catch` binding
  (#2333) and the `some(v)` binding of a match over a `string?` (#2750)
  each live for one block and may shadow a local of their name. Both exit
  frees were keyed by the name, so a `return` from inside the block freed
  the block's value and then tested the block's flag again for the outer
  local, whose value leaked. Such a binding is now renamed, with every use
  inside its construct, to a name of its own before code is generated, so
  each exit free reaches its own variable (#2746).

- **An array a `try` body writes can be passed to a `T[N]` parameter.** Its
  elements are volatile (#2690), and the callee's plain `E _param_a[N]`
  discarded the qualifier: a warning, an error under `-Werror`. A `T[N]`
  parameter is a value its callee copies, so such an argument (a local
  array, an array field of a local struct, a parameter array, for a
  function or a closure) is now copied into an array of the call's own,
  read through a volatile pointer; any other argument passes as before
  (#2723).

- **A closure frees its `string?` and `*StringSeq` locals.** A closure body
  ran the heap-string passes a function body runs but not their `string?`
  and `*StringSeq` counterparts, so such a local was declared with no
  ownership flag and no exit free, and every call of the closure leaked
  what it held. The closure body now runs all of them, as a function body
  does (#2761).

- **A closure can capture a `catch` binding or a `some(v)` binding.** A
  closure in a `catch e` handler that used `e`, or in the `some(v)` arm of
  a match over an optional that used `v`, read an undeclared name in its
  C body: capture discovery counted only declarations and parameters as
  the enclosing function's locals. It worked only when the function also
  had a local of the same name. Both bindings are captured now, typed as
  the panic's reason string and as the optional's value, and the
  closure's environment takes a reference of its own to a string it
  captures, as for any string local (#2769).

- **A hung test on macOS ends as `[TIMEOUT]` instead of holding the CI job.**
  The sweep bounded each test and each `make ci` stage with `timeout(1)` or
  `gtimeout`, and ran it with no limit where neither exists. GitHub's macOS
  runners ship no coreutils, so there every `.ae` test, shell test and stage
  ran unbounded: one hang held the job until GitHub's 6 hour ceiling, and a
  run cancelled after 40 minutes left no log naming the test. Where neither
  tool exists the bound is now perl, which every macOS has, with
  `timeout(1)`'s behaviour: the command runs in a process group of its own,
  which gets SIGTERM at the limit and SIGKILL after the grace period, and
  the status is 124 (137 when it had to be killed). The `ci` matrix and the
  Windows sweep jobs also carry a job-level `timeout-minutes`. The Windows
  legs split in two give the job that runs all of `make ci` a third of the
  sweep instead of half, so both halves finish together, and the macOS
  x86_64 leg runs two half sweeps (with the C unit tests on one), leaving
  the rest of `make ci` to the ARM64 leg, which runs it on macOS. The macOS
  leaks gate runs as two jobs, half the regression suite each: on a 3-core
  runner the whole suite took 19.5 minutes (#2772).

- **`ae build --namespace` removes its temp workspace.** The build writes the
  synthesized script, the describe stub and the generated C to
  `<temp>/aether_ns_<pid>`, and left that directory behind after every
  build, succeeded or failed, so a machine that builds namespaces often
  collected hundreds of them. It is now removed on every way out of the
  build, and one an earlier process with the same pid left is cleared before
  use (#2773).

### Performance

- **`ae build --trace`, and any build from a toolchain without libaether.a,
  compiles the runtime in parallel.** Such a source build handed every
  runtime source (about 90) to the one compiler command that links the
  program, which compiled them one after another. They are now compiled to
  objects first, as many at a time as there are processors, and the link
  takes the objects: message_trace's traced build went from 54 s to 17 s on
  an 8-processor Windows machine. A compile that fails, or a compiler that is
  a Windows batch file, falls back to the single command, which reports the
  error as before (#2757).

## [0.806.0]

### Fixed

- **A fixed-size array field can be bound from an array.** A struct literal
  given an array (`Shelf { names: arr }`), a store of one into the field
  (`s.names = arr`, `s.names = [...]`) and the same store into an actor's
  array state field (`names = arr`) emitted C that did not compile, since C
  neither initialises nor assigns an array from an array. The elements are
  copied one by one, each taken as the field keeps it: a `string[N]` field
  takes a reference to each element of another array and a copy of each
  element of a literal, a `fn[N]` field a reference to each closure, and an
  array of structs that own strings a value of its own per element, an
  actor's array state field of such structs included (it owns its
  elements, released by its `destroy_state`); a store takes every new
  element before storing any, so `s.names = [s.names[1], s.names[0]]`
  swaps, and gives back each element it replaces. The source must have the
  field's length: another length, an array literal longer than the field,
  or a slice or pointer, whose length is not known before the program
  runs, is a type error (a shorter literal zeroes the rest). Also fixed on
  the way: a store into a string field of an element of an array of
  structs (`items[i].name = v`) was a plain store, so a literal stored over
  an owned string was freed with the array (a crash) and a fresh string
  leaked (#2688).

- **A string read out of a `string[]` slice is copied where it escapes.**
  A function returning `xs[0]` of a slice handed the string back borrowed
  from whatever the slice viewed, and the caller held it after its owner
  let go of it: an array that owns its elements freed it on the next store
  or at its exit. A slice owns none of its elements, so a slot its element
  escapes to now takes a copy of its own, as for an element of an owning
  array (#2618): a return (directly, in an `if` or `match` arm, as a tuple
  position), a struct field, a container, or a call that hands its
  argument back. A local bound to a slice element (`t = s[i]`) still
  borrows it, so moving elements through a local
  (`t = s[0]; s[0] = s[1]; s[1] = t`) moves the pointers and keeps none,
  and the local is valid only while the element is; returned or added to
  a container, the local is copied in turn. A store into a slice element
  frees nothing and hands the storage what it stores, so moving an element
  through a copy (a function returning `s[i]`, stored back over another
  element) leaks the element it replaces; move elements through a local
  (#2689).

- **A `break` in a `switch` case leaves the switch, whatever its cases.** In
  a loop, a `switch` with a ranged case (`case 1..=5:`) is lowered to an
  if-chain, where the C `break` left the loop instead, and outside any loop
  it did not compile; a switch of plain cases left the switch but first ran
  the defers of the loop body around it, which then ran again when the body
  ended, and inside a `try` it popped the try's frame, which the try body
  popped again (the program aborted with "aether_try_pop on empty stack"). A
  `break` in an arm of a `match` on a sum type left the C switch that match
  lowers to, not the loop. A break now leaves the innermost loop or `switch`
  in every lowering, running the defers and popping the `try` frames of only
